exr:ii01-01: Show first that every term is below the proposed supremum, then use the Archimedean property to get terms arbitrarily close to it.
exr:ii01-02: Verify that 0 is a lower bound, then use the Archimedean property to put some 1/n below any prescribed positive number.
exr:ii01-06: Use induction on the number of elements, comparing the current maximum with the next element.
exr:ii02-01: Compute each norm directly from its defining formula; no topology or convergence theorem is needed.
exr:ii02-02: Check positivity and homogeneity directly, then use \(\lvert x_i+y_i\rvert\le \lvert x_i\rvert+\lvert y_i\rvert\) for the triangle inequality.
exr:ii03-01: Solve \(3/n<\varepsilon\) for \(n\), then choose an integer \(N\) so the inequality holds whenever \(n\ge N\).
exr:ii03-03: For a constant sequence every tail distance \(d(a_m,a_n)\) is exactly zero.
exr:ii04-01: For x in (0,1), choose a radius smaller than both x and 1-x.
exr:ii04-08: Use the extremal definitions: the interior lies inside the set, while the closure is a closed superset of it.
exr:ii05-01: Separate the cases x=z and x!=z; in the latter case at least one of d(x,y),d(y,z) equals 1.
exr:ii05-04: At a fixed point, split epsilon between the two summands and use continuity of each function.
exr:ii06-03: From an arbitrary open cover choose one member containing each of the finitely many points.
exr:ii06-04: A Cauchy sequence in a compact metric space has a convergent subsequence; use the Cauchy property to show the whole sequence has the same limit.
exr:ii07-05: A one-point space cannot be partitioned into two disjoint nonempty open pieces.
exr:ii08-03: Try L itself as the derivative of a linear map L; the remainder is identically zero.
exr:ii08-05: Add the two linearization formulas and combine their \(o(\lVert h\rVert)\) remainders.
exr:ii08-07: Test a one-variable counterexample such as \(f(x)=x^3\) at the origin; vanishing derivative need not imply an extremum.
exr:ii09-05: The inverse theorem gives a local diffeomorphism, and a diffeomorphism maps a sufficiently small neighborhood onto a neighborhood.
exr:ii10-01: The integral of the constant 1 over [0,2] is the rectangle area base times height.
exr:ii10-05: Split the interval at c and use additivity: integrate separately on [a,c] and [c,b].
exr:ii11-01: A uniform epsilon index works simultaneously for all x, so in particular it works at any one fixed x.
exr:ii11-05: Fix x first; then x/n is an ordinary numerical sequence tending to zero.
exr:ii12-04: Derivative data determine a function only up to an additive constant; one convergent value fixes that constant.
exr:ii13-03: Uniform convergence of the series means uniform convergence of its sequence of partial sums.
exr:ii13-06: The radius is the threshold separating guaranteed convergence inside from divergence outside; endpoints must be checked separately.
exr:ii14-04: A trigonometric polynomial is a finite linear combination of 1, cos(nx), and sin(nx).
exr:ii14-05: Use the nonnegativity of the squared norm after subtracting the finite orthogonal projection.
exr:ii15-02: Yes: the M-test gives uniform convergence of the continuous partial sums, and uniform limits preserve continuity.
exr:ii15-04: Use the Cantor function: it is constant on each removed interval but still increases from 0 to 1.
exr:ii16-03: If x and y are fixed points, compare d(x,y)=d(Tx,Ty) with q d(x,y).
exr:ii16-05: The Picard iterates are Cauchy; completeness is exactly what turns that Cauchy sequence into a limit in the space.
exr:ii17-01: Apply the interval fixed-point theorem, or apply the intermediate-value theorem to f(x)-x.
exr:ii17-03: No. The identity map already has every point as a fixed point.
exr:ii18-01: Rewrite f=g+Kf as (I-K)f=g; when I-K is invertible this determines the solution.
exr:ii18-03: Use the sup norm because a uniform kernel bound lets \(\lVert f\rVert_\infty\) factor out of the integral estimate.
exr:ii19-02: Picard--Lindelof gives local uniqueness once continuity and a local Lipschitz condition in y are verified.
exr:ii19-04: Subtract two integral equations and apply Gronwall to the absolute difference.
exr:ii20-02: A degree-at-most-n polynomial is uniquely determined by n+1 values at distinct nodes.
exr:ii20-06: Subtract two candidates; their difference would have n+1 distinct zeros but degree at most n.
exr:ii21-01: Weierstrass approximation is uniform: the error is measured in the sup norm on the compact interval.
exr:ii21-06: Density means every epsilon-ball around a continuous function contains a polynomial; it does not mean exact equality.
exr:ii22-04: The polynomial space of degree at most n has dimension n+1, so minimax alternation requires n+2 ordered extreme points.
exr:ii22-08: No. Minimax minimizes the largest error, whereas least squares minimizes an integrated squared error.
exr:ii23-05: Assume a better competitor exists; alternating inequalities force the difference polynomial to have too many sign changes and hence too many zeros.
exr:ii24-06: Test the rule on \(x^4\); degree-three exactness does not extend automatically to degree four.
exr:ii25-06: Use \(p_nq_{n-1}-p_{n-1}q_n=(-1)^{n-1}\); taking absolute values gives the adjacent-convergent separation.
exr:ii25-08: Use the exact continued-fraction error formula; the neighboring-denominator bound is sharper than a generic order statement.
